area: Area IV. Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds
objective: By the end of this lesson you can plan a soft-field departure with corrected performance numbers, explain how ground effect and weight transfer get you airborne, and fly the takeoff and climb to commercial standards, holding VX or VY within 5 knots.
why: About 1 in 5 general aviation accidents happen during takeoff and departure climb, and more than half of those come from pilot failure [[24:133|AFH 6-1]]. On grass, mud or snow the airplane can lift off and then fail to climb out of ground effect, so the numbers and the technique both have to be right [[24:143|AFH 6-11]].

prereading.what: Ground effect on takeoff, VX and VY, short-field contrast, soft/rough-field takeoff and its common errors, rejected takeoff, engine failure, noise abatement.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 6, 6-10 to 6-14

prereading.what: Ground effect: airflow, lift coefficient, thrust required, instrument errors and what happens as you leave it.
prereading.label: PHAK Ch 5, 5-11 to 5-12

prereading.what: Climb performance: angle versus rate of climb, weight and altitude effects, absolute and service ceiling.
prereading.label: PHAK Ch 11, 11-6 to 11-9

prereading.what: Region of reversed command, runway surface and slope, and how weight, wind, speed and density altitude change takeoff distance.
prereading.label: PHAK Ch 11, 11-11 to 11-16

prereading.what: Reading takeoff distance charts, interpolating, and applying the wind and grass-runway notes.
prereading.label: PHAK Ch 11, 11-20 to 11-22

prereading.what: The four parts of the left-turning tendency.
prereading.label: PHAK Ch 5, 5-30 to 5-32

warmup: Your POH takeoff chart says you need 1,325 feet of ground roll, and the grass strip is 2,000 feet long. The chart header says "paved level runway." Is 2,000 feet enough? What would you want to know before you answer?

key_terms.def: A takeoff surface such as tall grass, soft sand, mud or snow that drags on the wheels and slows acceleration [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
Moving the airplane's weight from the wheels to the wings as early as possible by holding a nose-high attitude through the roll [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
Improved performance close to the surface, normally up to about one wingspan high, because the ground cuts upwash, downwash and wingtip vortices [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].
Drag that comes from making lift. It is largest at low speed and high angle of attack [[1:108|PHAK 5-11]].
Best angle of climb speed: the most altitude for a given distance over the ground [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].
Best rate of climb speed: the most altitude per unit of time [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].
The altitude where there is no excess power, only one speed holds level flight, and the rate of climb is zero. VX and VY meet there [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]].
Slow flight where a lower airspeed needs more power to hold altitude [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]].
A point on the runway, picked before takeoff, where you should be airborne. Not airborne there means you reject the takeoff [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].
At high angle of attack the down-moving propeller blade makes more thrust, so the nose yaws left [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].

body.p: Tall grass, soft sand, mud and snow all add drag. A soft-field takeoff aims to get airborne as quickly as possible to get rid of that drag, and you may still need to climb over an obstacle [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

Long, wet grass can slow you so much that a normal takeoff technique never reaches takeoff speed [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. The answer is weight transfer: hold a relatively high angle of attack, nose-high, as early as possible. As speed builds, the wings carry more and more of the weight, so the wheels feel less of the surface drag [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

head: Short-field takeoff
Soft-field takeoff
rows: Full weight on the main wheels, low-drag attitude [[24:143|AFH 6-11]]
Nose-wheel up early, nose-high attitude held [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]
Flies itself off below a safe climb speed [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]
Lower the nose, stay in ground effect to at least VX [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]

body.p: Configuration for the takeoff:

bullets: Flaps: lower them before the roll if the manufacturer recommends it. They add lift and move the weight to the wings sooner [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
Keep moving: line up with continuous motion and enough power. Stopping on mud or snow can bog the airplane down [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
Gear and flaps up: after a positive rate of climb at VY, or after you clear the obstacle. After wet snow or slush, leave the gear down for a bit so it can air-dry [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
The POH/AFM wins: if a handbook differs from the manufacturer, use the manufacturer's procedure [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].

callout.text: Commercial standard: hold VX or VY within 5 knots, plus or minus, during the climb and up to a safe maneuvering altitude (ACS CA.IV.C.S10, CA.IV.C.S12). The private standard was +10/-5, so you lose the extra 5 knots on the fast side.

check.q: Why does a soft-field takeoff lift the nose-wheel early instead of rolling level like a short-field takeoff?
check.a: The nose-high attitude lets the wings take the weight early, which cuts the drag from the soft surface. A short field is firm, so you roll in the low-drag attitude instead [[24:145|AFH 6-13]] [[24:143|AFH 6-11]].

chunks.title: Ground effect: what it gives and what it takes back

body.p: Near the ground, the surface blocks the up-and-down part of the airflow. Upwash, downwash and wingtip vortices shrink [[1:108|PHAK 5-11]]. Two things follow [[1:108|PHAK 5-11]]:

bullets: The wing needs a lower angle of attack for the same lift coefficient. Hold the same angle of attack and you get more lift.
Induced drag drops. Induced drag is the big drag at low speed, so the thrust you need at low speed drops a lot.

body.p: The wing has to be very close to the ground for a big effect [[1:108|PHAK 5-11]]. Example for a 36-foot wingspan:

In ground effect, pressure at the static source goes up. The airspeed indicator and altimeter read a little low, and the VSI usually shows a descent [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]. So the airplane can be flying at an indicated airspeed lower than it normally needs [[1:108|PHAK 5-11]].
Climbing out of ground effect reverses all of this. The airplane [[1:109|PHAK 5-12]] [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]:

bullets: Needs more angle of attack for the same lift coefficient.
Gets more induced drag and needs more thrust.
Becomes less stable and pitches nose-up, with more downwash on the tail.
Shows a higher indicated airspeed as static pressure drops.

callout.text: Ground effect can fool you. The airplane may seem able to take off well below the recommended speed. Climb out of ground effect short of speed and the extra drag can leave you with a marginal climb, or settle you back onto the runway when heavy, hot and high [[1:109|PHAK 5-12]].

check.q: As you climb out of ground effect, which way does the nose want to go, and what happens to indicated airspeed?
check.a: The nose pitches up (more downwash on the tail), and indicated airspeed reads higher because static pressure drops [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

chunks.title: Surface condition and the performance chart

body.p: Performance charts usually assume a paved, level, smooth, dry runway [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]]. A grass strip is none of those. Any surface that is not hard and smooth makes the ground roll longer, because tires sink into soft, grassy or muddy ground. Mud, snow and standing water also slow your acceleration [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].
Find the runway surface and slope in the Chart Supplement [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]] [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]]. An upsloping runway slows acceleration and lengthens the ground run [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]].
Many POH charts carry notes that correct the numbers for wind and surface. Here is the PHAK sample short-field table:

bullets: Find your weight row, then your pressure altitude, then your temperature column [[1:277|PHAK 11-21]].
Between two lines? Average them (interpolate). Rounding to the more adverse condition gives a small safety margin [[1:276|PHAK 11-20]].
Wind note: cut distances 10 percent for each 9 knots of headwind. With a tailwind up to 10 knots, add 10 percent for each 2 knots [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]].
Grass note: on a dry grass runway, add 15 percent of the ground roll figure [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]].

body.p: Chart values from [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]] and [[1:277|PHAK 11-21]]. The note says to increase the distances, so the same 199 ft goes on both columns.

callout.text: The note says dry grass. Long wet grass, mud or snow can be far worse, and may keep you from ever reaching takeoff speed [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. Many airplanes cannot take off safely at maximum gross weight at some altitudes and temperatures [[24:143|AFH 6-11]]. If the corrected number is close, it is not good enough.

check.q: Chart ground roll is 1,000 ft and total over 50 ft is 1,800 ft. Using the sample dry-grass note, what are the new numbers?
check.a: Add 15 percent of the ground roll (150 ft) to both: 1,150 ft ground roll and 1,950 ft total [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]].

chunks.title: Wind, weight, speed and density altitude

body.p: Check the POH/AFM performance charts before you go and decide whether the airplane can make a safe takeoff and climb in these conditions [[24:133|AFH 6-1]]. These rules of thumb show how big each factor is:

head: Change
Effect
rows: 5% higher takeoff speed, at least 9% less acceleration, at least 21% more distance [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]]
Same indicated airspeed but higher true airspeed at lift-off, and less thrust [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]]

callout.text: "Ten in, twenty-one out": a tailwind of 10 percent of takeoff speed, 10 percent more weight, or a lift-off 10 percent too fast each adds about 21 percent to the takeoff distance (at least 21 percent for weight) [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]] [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]].

body.p: The worst takeoffs combine high weight, high altitude, high temperature and an unfavorable wind. Work out the takeoff distance from the POH no matter how long the runway is [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]].

Tailwind: take off into the wind when you can. A headwind gives you airspeed before you move and lowers the groundspeed you need [[24:135|AFH 6-3]]. If you must use a tailwind, first confirm the POH/AFM approves it and that you have the performance and the runway [[24:135|AFH 6-3]].
Heavy or hot also changes the climb: the climb pitch attitude is lower when the airplane is heavy or density altitude limits power [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

check.q: Why does a hot, high-elevation strip need a longer roll even though you lift off at the normal indicated airspeed?
check.a: You need a higher true airspeed (more groundspeed) for the same indicated airspeed, and the engine makes less thrust to get you there [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]].

chunks.title: VX, VY and clearing the obstacle

body.p: VX gives the greatest altitude gain for a given distance over the ground. VY gives the greatest gain per unit of time. VX is usually a little slower than VY [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

The PHAK compares them with one airplane at full throttle. At VX it reaches 1,000 feet in 30 seconds but covers only 3,000 feet over the ground. At VY it reaches 1,500 feet in 30 seconds but covers 6,000 feet [[1:263|PHAK 11-7]] [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]]. VX is the steep path; VY is the fast path.

In a propeller airplane, the best angle of climb usually comes at a speed below best lift/drag, and often just above the stall speed [[1:263|PHAK 11-7]]. So VX leaves you little margin. Fly it only while you need it.

bullets: Altitude: as you climb, the climb speeds change and finally meet at the absolute ceiling [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]]. On the PHAK chart, VX rises and VY falls with altitude [[1:265|PHAK Figure 11-10]].
Weight: a heavier airplane has a lower best rate of climb and needs a higher climb speed to get it [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]].
Precision: in some airplanes, 5 knots off the recommended speed causes a significant loss of climb performance [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]. That is why the commercial standard is a tight 5 knots.

body.p: Soft-field sequence: stay in ground effect until at least VX. If an obstacle must be cleared, climb at VX until it is cleared, then pitch for VY, retract gear and flaps, and reduce to climb power [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

callout.text: Your chart's "total to clear 50 ft" column assumes you fly the book speeds [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]]. If the trees are taller than 50 feet, that column does not prove you clear them.

check.q: There are no obstacles past the end of the strip. Which speed do you climb at after accelerating in ground effect, and why?
check.a: VY. You still stay in ground effect to at least VX [[24:145|AFH 6-13]], but with nothing to clear, VY gives the most altitude in the least time [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

chunks.title: Settling back: the trap right after lift-off

body.p: Right after lift-off, as the airplane moves out of ground effect, it tends to settle back onto the surface, even with full power. That is why it must stay in ground effect until at least VX [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

Pulling the airplane off too early, or climbing too steeply, can put it back on the runway or into obstacles. Even if it stays airborne, the climb stays flat until VX [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]. Lifting off below the recommended speed means more drag, and at full power the only way to cut drag is to lower the pitch, which costs altitude [[24:143|AFH 6-11]].

The power-required curve shows why. Below best endurance speed you are in the region of reversed command: slower needs more power [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]]. Climb out of ground effect without normal climb attitude and airspeed and you can enter this region at a dangerously low altitude. Even full power may not climb or hold altitude. The only fix is to lower the pitch to gain speed, losing altitude [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].

The cure is to reduce angle of attack and reach normal airspeed before you fly out of ground effect [[24:143|AFH 6-11]]. In marginal conditions, take off at the speed the manufacturer recommends for adequate initial climb [[24:143|AFH 6-11]].

callout.text: You can also settle back the other way. Let the nose drop too far after lift-off and the angle of attack and lift fall until the wing cannot hold the airplane up [[24:137|AFH 6-5]]. Lower the nose gently, just enough to hold the wheels clear [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

check.q: At full power, just off the grass, the airplane will not climb and the stall horn chirps. What is the only way out?
check.a: Lower the pitch to gain airspeed and reduce drag, accepting some altitude loss; you are likely in the region of reversed command [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]] [[24:143|AFH 6-11]].

chunks.title: Left-turning tendencies in a nose-high roll

body.p: "Torque" is really four separate effects [[1:127|PHAK 5-30]]. A soft-field takeoff, at full power, slow and nose-high, brings out all of them:

head: Effect
Why it shows up on a soft-field takeoff
rows: On the ground it loads the left main wheel, adding drag and a left turn. Ground surface condition is one of the things that changes how strong it is [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]]
Strongest at high propeller speed and low forward speed, like the start of the roll [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]]
Any pitch change makes a yaw, so raising the nose-wheel or lowering the nose after lift-off can yaw the airplane [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]]
High angle of attack makes the down-moving blade bite harder and yaws the nose left [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]]

body.p: Torque also tries to roll the airplane, most of all just as the wheels leave the surface [[24:137|AFH 6-5]]. Keep the wings level and stay coordinated with rudder as you level off in ground effect.

callout.text: Add power smoothly: abrupt power can yaw the airplane sharply left. Steer with rudder, not brakes. Brakes slow acceleration and lengthen the takeoff [[24:135|AFH 6-3]], which is the last thing you want on grass.

check.q: Which two left-turning effects are strongest at full power, low speed and a high angle of attack?
check.a: Corkscrew slipstream (high power, low speed) and P-factor (high angle of attack) [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]] [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].

bullets: 1. Before the runway: run the corrected performance numbers, then finish the run-up and before-takeoff checklists on firm ground [[24:133|AFH 6-1]]. Set flaps as the POH says [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
2. Announce on the CTAF, or get your takeoff clearance before taxiing onto the runway at a towered field [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].
3. Check the wind indicators and make sure the approach and takeoff paths are clear [[24:138|AFH 6-6]] [[24:133|AFH 6-1]]. Confirm the heading matches the runway [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]].
4. Taxi onto the runway without stopping, crosswind aileron in, and line up on the centerline [[24:145|AFH 6-13]] [[24:138|AFH 6-6]].
5. Add takeoff power smoothly and as fast as the engine accepts it. Check the engine instruments [[24:145|AFH 6-13]] [[24:135|AFH 6-3]].
6. Hold enough back pressure for a positive angle of attack and a light nose-wheel. Keep that nose-high attitude so the wings take the weight [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
7. Let the airplane fly itself off, below a safe climb speed [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
8. Lower the nose gently with the wheels just clear of the surface. Accelerate in ground effect to at least VX [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
9. Pitch for VX if there is an obstacle, VY if not. Expect a pitch-up as you leave ground effect [[24:145|AFH 6-13]] [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].
10. After a positive rate of climb and VY (or once clear of the obstacle), retract gear and flaps, or as the manufacturer says. After slush, leave the gear down briefly [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
11. Keep takeoff power to at least 500 feet above terrain or obstacles, then set climb power and trim [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].
12. Track the extended centerline with a crab for drift, and fly any noise abatement procedure [[24:140|AFH 6-8]] [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

head: ACS item
Commercial standard
rows: Taxi into position and align on centerline without stopping, throttle smoothly to takeoff power (ACS CA.IV.C.S6)
Pitch attitude that moves the weight to the wings as rapidly as possible (ACS CA.IV.C.S8)
Lowest possible airspeed, then stay in ground effect while accelerating to VX or VY (ACS CA.IV.C.S9)
After a verified positive rate of climb, or per the manufacturer (ACS CA.IV.C.S11)

callout.text: Keep it ROLLING, keep it LIGHT, keep it LOW, then let it GO: never stop, nose-wheel light, level in ground effect, climb at VX or VY.

check.q: On the checkride your VY is 79 knots. What airspeed range keeps you within the commercial standard?
check.a: 74 to 84 knots, ±5 knots (ACS CA.IV.C.S10). Aim for 79: in some airplanes 5 knots off hurts climb a lot [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

body.p: The AFH lists these soft/rough-field errors [[24:145|AFH 6-13]] [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. Each one comes with its fix:

head: Error
Fix
rows: No review of AFM/POH and performance charts
Correct the chart for surface, wind and weight before you taxi
Scan the approach and takeoff paths before you roll onto the runway
Too little back pressure early in the roll
Set the nose-high attitude as soon as the elevator works
Quick look at RPM and engine gauges once power is set
Right rudder for the left-turning tendencies; no brakes
Level off low enough to stay in ground effect
Abrupt or too much elevator at level-off
Lower the nose gently, just enough to hold the wheels clear
Letting it mush or settle back
Hold the attitude that keeps you just off the surface
Climbing out of ground effect too slow
Surprised by the pitch-up leaving ground effect
Expect it; use forward pressure and trim

body.p: At the commercial level, the examiner also watches the climb speed. Fly attitude first: set the pitch on the horizon, hold it, then check the airspeed indicator. Do not chase the needle [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

check.q: After lift-off you push the nose over firmly to level off, and the wheels touch the grass again. Which listed error is this?
check.a: Abrupt or excessive elevator while leveling off to accelerate, which let the airplane settle back [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

chunks.title: Risk: runway, wind, windshear and wake

body.p: Pick the runway on four things: your skill, the airplane's corrected performance, the distance you have, and the wind. Assess the flight's risk honestly against your experience [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]], and predict the takeoff distance from the POH regardless of runway length [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]].

head: Hazard
What it does on a soft field
What you do
rows: Deflected ailerons and rudder add drag, so expect less takeoff performance [[24:138|AFH 6-6]]. Skipping sideways loads the gear hard [[24:139|AFH 6-7]]
Full aileron into the wind at the start, rudder to stay straight, correction set before lift-off, then crab [[24:138|AFH 6-6]] [[24:140|AFH 6-8]]
A headwind turning to tailwind cuts airspeed and performance [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. On the runway, the only sign may be slow airspeed buildup, hidden by gusts [[28:270|AWH 22-15]]
Expect it near fronts, thunderstorms, inversions and upper winds over 25 knots; be ready to react at once [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]
About 21% more distance at 10% of takeoff speed [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]]
Only if the POH approves it and the numbers work [[24:135|AFH 6-3]]
Near the ground, vortices drift sideways at 2-3 knots [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]
Rotate before the larger airplane's rotation point and climb above its path; wait at least 2 minutes after its low approach or touch-and-go [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]
Longer roll; may never reach takeoff speed [[24:145|AFH 6-13]] [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]]
Correct the chart, add margin, use soft-field technique

body.p: The AFH gives two pieces of advice you have to weigh together. In a significant crosswind, it says to hold the main wheels on slightly longer for a smooth but definite lift-off, because settling back while drifting can damage the gear [[24:139|AFH 6-7]]. On a soft field, the airplane flies itself off below a safe climb speed and then stays in ground effect [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. The AFH does not say how to combine the two, so follow your POH and talk it through with your instructor. Either way, set and hold your crosswind correction before lift-off [[24:140|AFH 6-8]].

Gusts: the AFH advises an extra margin of speed before leaving the ground in strong, gusty wind, since a sudden lull at normal takeoff speed can cost you control or stall the airplane [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

Finding the wind: ATC gives it at a towered field. Otherwise use the CTAF or FSS, but still check the windsock, because CTAF information may not be accurate [[1:354|PHAK 14-20]]. No indicator at all? Smoke drift shows direction, and leaves, twigs and flags hint at speed [[34:227|AIM TBL 10-2-3]].

check.q: A larger airplane just made a low approach over your grass runway in a light quartering wind. What does the AIM recommend?
check.a: Wait at least 2 minutes before you take off, because its vortices can settle and drift along the runway [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

chunks.title: Risk: rejected takeoff, engine failure and staying ahead

body.p: Rejected takeoff. Before you roll, pick the point on the runway where you should be airborne. Not airborne there? Stop at once [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. The POH takeoff and landing ground rolls added together give a good estimate of the runway you need to accelerate and then stop [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. Use your corrected (grass) ground roll in that sum.

bullets: Reasons to reject: a sick engine, poor acceleration, a runway incursion, or a traffic conflict [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].
How: power to idle, maximum braking while keeping directional control. For a fire, mixture to idle cutoff and magnetos off. Always follow the POH [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

For soft-field landings, the AFH says to avoid braking, because it can load the nose gear and make the nose-wheel dig in, and the soft surface itself slows the airplane [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. It gives no special method for a rejected takeoff on a soft surface, so follow the POH.

body.p: Engine failure after lift-off. Plan it before takeoff: know your preferred direction for an emergency turn based on the departure path, altitude, wind and terrain [[24:133|AFH 6-1]]. If it happens, you have only seconds. In a climb attitude without power you are at or near a stall, and you may still be holding right rudder. Lower the nose at once, center the rudder for coordinated flight, and glide to a landing area, preferably straight ahead. Turn back only if trained for it and high enough [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

Low-altitude stall, spin and CFIT. Many stall/spin accidents happen in takeoff and climb-out; premature flap retraction is one cause [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104b]]. Never raise the flaps or gear before a positive rate of climb and a safe altitude [[1:109|PHAK 5-12]], and raise flaps in steps to avoid a sudden loss of lift [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]. High density altitude is a CFIT factor [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]: an airplane that cannot climb out of ground effect may not clear obstructions [[24:143|AFH 6-11]].

Collision hazards. Make sure the approach and takeoff paths are clear before you take the runway [[24:133|AFH 6-1]], and keep scanning in the climb [[24:138|AFH 6-6]]. Monitor the CTAF from startup, through taxi and after departure [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.4.2]].

Distractions. Many flight deck distractions start as a small problem, like a gauge that reads wrong [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. Until you are clear of obstacles, keep your eyes outside, not on the flap or gear handle [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]. Brief a sterile flight deck from departure until you are clear of the local airspace [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].

callout.text: Before every soft-field takeoff, say three things out loud: the abort point, the corrected distance, and where you will land if the engine quits.

check.q: Your POH ground roll is 1,524 ft (corrected for grass) and the landing ground roll is 650 ft. About how much runway do you need to accelerate and stop?

scenario.title: A hot afternoon at a short grass strip
scenario.setup: You are a commercial pilot repositioning an airplane that uses the PHAK sample chart (Figure 11-24) out of a dry turf strip, 2,200 feet long, at 3,000 feet pressure altitude. It is 30 °C. With you and full bags the airplane weighs 2,400 lb. Trees about 50 feet tall line the far end of Runway 09; Runway 27 has open fields. Wind is from 090 at 9 knots. The owner, riding along, keeps asking about his business deal as you taxi, and a thunderstorm is building about 15 miles west.

questions.q: Work out the distance to clear a 50-foot obstacle on Runway 09. Does it fit?
questions.a: Chart: ground roll 1,325 ft, total 2,480 ft [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]]. Dry grass adds 15% of the ground roll, 199 ft, so 2,679 ft. The 9-knot headwind cuts it 10%, to about 2,411 ft [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]]. That is more than the 2,200 ft strip, so no.

questions.q: Why not just use Runway 27 toward the open fields?
questions.a: That is a 9-knot tailwind. The chart note covers tailwinds up to 10 knots and adds 10% for each 2 knots, about 45% here [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]], and the POH must approve tailwind takeoffs [[24:135|AFH 6-3]]. It makes the distance worse, not better.

questions.q: What could make the takeoff work?
questions.a: Less weight or cooler air. Leave the bags to get down to 2,200 lb: the chart gives 1,070 ft and 1,975 ft. Add 15% of the ground roll for grass (161 ft) to get 2,136 ft, then take off 10% for the 9-knot headwind: about 1,922 ft [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]]. That fits, but with only about 280 ft to spare, and it counts on the headwind holding. Cooler evening air adds margin. Remember a hot, heavy airplane may lift off and not climb out of ground effect [[24:143|AFH 6-11]].

questions.q: The storm is closer now and the windsock is swinging. What is the risk?
questions.a: Low-level windshear comes with thunderstorms; a headwind turning to tailwind cuts airspeed and performance [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. On the roll, slow airspeed buildup may be the only sign [[28:270|AWH 22-15]]. On a marginal strip, that is a reason to wait.

questions.q: You decide to go at 2,200 lb in the cool evening. What do you brief before rolling?
questions.a: An abort point where you must be airborne [[24:146|AFH 6-14]], the engine-failure landing area and turn direction [[24:133|AFH 6-1]], a CTAF call and a scan of both paths [[24:133|AFH 6-1]], and VX until the trees are cleared [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

questions.q: How do you handle the owner's chatter?
questions.a: Ask for a sterile flight deck from departure until clear of the local airspace [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]. Distractions divert attention from flying and scanning [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

skills.do: Complete the run-up and before-takeoff checklists before taxiing onto the runway, including corrected performance numbers.
skills.practice: Finish every item while stopped on firm ground, so you never have to stop on the soft runway [[24:133|AFH 6-1]] [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

skills.do: Make the right radio calls: a CTAF announcement, or a takeoff clearance at a towered airport.
skills.practice: Monitor the CTAF from startup through taxi and after departure [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.4.2]]; get the clearance before entering the runway at a towered field [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].

skills.do: Verify you are on the assigned or correct runway.
skills.practice: Set the heading bug to the runway heading and check the heading against it before adding power [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]].

skills.do: State the wind direction, with or without a wind indicator.
skills.practice: Use the windsock even when CTAF gives a wind [[1:354|PHAK 14-20]]; with none, read smoke, leaves and flags [[34:227|AIM TBL 10-2-3]].

skills.do: Position the flight controls for the wind.
skills.practice: Full aileron into a crosswind at the start of the roll, easing off as the ailerons become effective [[24:138|AFH 6-6]] [[24:140|AFH 6-8]].

skills.do: Clear the area, hold the control inputs, taxi into position and align on the centerline without stopping, while advancing the throttle smoothly to takeoff power.
skills.practice: Practice a rolling line-up with enough power to keep moving, then set back pressure as the roll begins [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

skills.do: Confirm takeoff power and normal engine and flight instrument indications.
skills.practice: Check the engine instruments for signs of a malfunction early in the roll [[24:135|AFH 6-3]], glance that the airspeed is rising, then eyes outside.

skills.do: Set and hold a pitch attitude that moves the weight from wheels to wings as rapidly as possible.
skills.practice: Learn the nose-high picture against the horizon with your instructor and hold it steady through the roll [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

skills.do: Lift off at the lowest possible airspeed and stay in ground effect while accelerating to VX or VY.
skills.practice: On a long runway, practice the gentle level-off with the wheels just clear of the surface [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

skills.do: Pitch for VX or VY and hold the selected speed ±5 knots during the climb (ACS CA.IV.C.S10).
skills.practice: Set the attitude first, hold it, then check airspeed and adjust [[24:137|AFH 6-5]]. Precision matters: 5 knots off can hurt climb a lot [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

skills.do: Configure the airplane after a verified positive rate of climb, or as the manufacturer says.
skills.practice: Call "positive rate" before touching flaps or gear [[1:109|PHAK 5-12]]; after slush, delay gear retraction [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

skills.do: Hold VX or VY ±5 knots up to a safe maneuvering altitude (ACS CA.IV.C.S12).
skills.practice: Keep takeoff power to at least 500 feet above terrain or obstacles, then set climb power and trim [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

skills.do: Keep directional control and wind-drift correction through the takeoff and climb.
skills.practice: Right rudder for the left-turning tendencies, then crab to stay over the extended centerline [[24:135|AFH 6-3]] [[24:140|AFH 6-8]].

skills.do: Comply with noise abatement procedures, as applicable.
skills.practice: Look them up in the Chart Supplement or local publications, or ask the tower [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

quiz.q: Your VY is 79 knots. Which climb airspeed band meets the commercial ACS standard?
options: 74 to 84 knots
74 to 89 knots
69 to 89 knots
77 to 81 knots
quiz.why: The commercial standard is ±5 knots (ACS CA.IV.C.S10), so 74 to 84. The private +10/-5 band (74 to 89) no longer applies. Fly it exactly: 5 knots off can cost a lot of climb [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

quiz.q: Using the sample chart's dry-grass note, a ground roll of 1,000 ft and a total over 50 ft of 1,900 ft become:
options: 1,150 ft and 2,185 ft
1,200 ft and 2,280 ft
1,150 ft and 1,900 ft
1,150 ft and 2,050 ft
quiz.why: Add 15% of the ground roll figure (150 ft) to the distances: 1,150 ft and 2,050 ft [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]]. Adding 15% of the total figure, or 20%, are common slips.

quiz.q: In ground effect, if you hold the same angle of attack, the lift coefficient:
options: Decreases
Increases
Stays the same
Drops to zero
quiz.why: Ground effect cuts induced angle of attack, so at a constant angle of attack the lift coefficient increases [[1:108|PHAK 5-11]].

quiz.q: Besides more drag and more required angle of attack, the PHAK says an airplane leaving ground effect experiences:
options: More stability and a nose-down moment
A rise in static pressure
Less stability and a nose-up moment
A drop in indicated airspeed
quiz.why: Leaving ground effect brings a decrease in stability, a nose-up change in moment, and lower static pressure with higher indicated airspeed [[1:109|PHAK 5-12]].

quiz.q: In a propeller airplane, the best angle of climb usually occurs at:
options: A speed above best lift/drag
Exactly best lift/drag
The same speed as VY
A speed below best lift/drag, often just above stall
quiz.why: Maximum excess thrust in a propeller airplane normally comes below L/D max and frequently just above stall speed [[1:263|PHAK 11-7]]. That is why VX leaves little margin.

quiz.q: As you climb toward the absolute ceiling, how do VX and VY change?
options: VX increases and VY decreases until they meet
Both increase together
Both decrease together
VX decreases and VY increases
quiz.why: The climb speeds converge at the absolute ceiling [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]]. On the PHAK chart, VX rises and VY falls with altitude [[1:265|PHAK Figure 11-10]].

quiz.q: What does added weight do to climb performance?
options: Raises the best rate of climb and lowers the climb speed
Lowers the best rate of climb and needs a higher climb speed
No change, as long as you use full power
Lowers only VX, not VY
quiz.why: More weight reduces the maximum rate of climb, and the airplane must fly a higher climb speed to get that smaller peak [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]].

quiz.q: In the region of reversed command, holding altitude at a slower airspeed requires:
options: Less power
The same power
More power
Idle power
quiz.why: Below the speed for minimum power, a lower airspeed needs a higher power setting to hold altitude [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]].

quiz.q: On the takeoff roll, how strongly torque reaction pulls left depends partly on:
options: The condition of the ground surface
The altimeter setting
The flap setting only
The wind direction only
quiz.why: Torque reaction loads the left main wheel. Its strength depends on engine size and power, propeller size and RPM, airplane size, and the condition of the ground surface [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].

takeaways: Correct the chart first: it assumes a paved, dry runway, and grass, wind and weight change the answer [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].
Never stop on the soft surface; get the nose-wheel light and the weight on the wings early.
Lift off slow, then stay in ground effect to at least VX. Climbing out early can leave you unable to climb.
VX to clear the obstacle, then VY, each held ±5 knots (ACS CA.IV.C.S10).
Pick an abort point, and know where you will land if the engine quits.
Crosswind costs takeoff performance, gusts call for extra speed, windshear cuts airspeed, and wake can linger: weigh them all when you pick the runway and the time.
cfi_notes: Have the student correct a real POH chart for the strip, wind and weight on every soft-field lesson; examiners often ask for the numbers before the flight.
The tighter commercial band (±5 knots, ACS CA.IV.C.S10) catches students who were comfortable fast at the private level. Drill attitude-first climbs [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].
The PHAK sample chart's grass note adds 15% of the ground roll to both distances [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]]. Students often add 15% of the total instead; check their work.
Watch the level-off: too high leaves ground effect, too abrupt touches back down. Both are on the AFH error list [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

Discuss the strong-crosswind advice (hold the main wheels on slightly longer, AFH 6-7) next to the soft-field lift-off below a safe climb speed [[24:139|AFH 6-7]] [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. No source here says how to blend them, so treat it as a judgment discussion and follow the POH.
PHAK 12-11 refers pilots to AC 00-54 for windshear escape technique. That AC is not in this lesson's sources; use the AWH material and the POH [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].
Tailwheel students: AFH 14-4 says the elevator is usually best full up while taxiing onto a soft runway, and the tail is kept very low during the roll [[24:290|AFH 14-4]].
gaps: Airplane-specific flap setting, lift-off speed, VX/VY and soft-surface corrections come from the POH/AFM; these sources give only the PHAK sample chart and its dry-grass note.
No source here gives correction factors for wet grass, mud, sand or snow, only that they lengthen the roll and may prevent reaching takeoff speed.
No source gives a specific technique for rejecting a takeoff on a soft surface; AFH 6-14 is general and AFH 9-24 covers soft-field braking only for landing.
The sources do not say how to combine the AFH strong-crosswind advice (hold the wheels on longer) with the soft-field low-speed lift-off.
The PHAK points to AC 00-54 for windshear escape, which is not among the uploaded sources; AWH 22-15 discusses runway encounters mainly for large airplanes.
Noise abatement procedures are airport-specific (Chart Supplement, local publications).

activities.title: True or false: ground effect
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: With the wing at a height equal to its span, induced drag is cut by almost half.
cards.why: No. At one wingspan the cut is only 1.4 percent. You need to be at 1/10 of the span to get 47.6 percent [[1:108|PHAK 5-11]].

cards.s: In ground effect the airspeed indicator usually reads a little low.
cards.why: Yes. Static source pressure rises, so the airspeed indicator and altimeter read slightly low [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

cards.s: Ground effect matters most at low speed, because induced drag is the main drag there.
cards.why: Yes. Induced drag dominates at low speed, so cutting it greatly lowers the thrust required [[1:108|PHAK 5-11]] [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

cards.s: As you climb out of ground effect, you need less angle of attack for the same lift.
cards.why: No. You need more angle of attack to keep the same lift coefficient [[1:109|PHAK 5-12]].

cards.s: When heavy, hot and high, an airplane may lift off in ground effect but be unable to climb out of it.
cards.why: Yes. A deficiency of speed can let it get airborne but not sustain flight out of ground effect, so it settles back [[1:109|PHAK 5-12]].

cards.s: As the airplane leaves ground effect, the nose tends to drop.
cards.why: No. It pitches up, because downwash at the tail increases, and it needs less elevator travel [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

activities.title: Read the takeoff chart
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.

pins.label: Distance to clear 50 ft at 3,000 ft and 30 °C

activities.title: Correct the numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Sample chart: 2,400 lb, 3,000 ft, 30 °C gives a ground roll of 1,325 ft. The runway is dry grass. Add 15% of the ground roll. What is the corrected ground roll?
Same conditions: the total to clear a 50-ft obstacle is 2,480 ft. Apply the same dry-grass correction (15% of the 1,325-ft ground roll). What is the corrected total?
items.why: The note adds 15% of the ground roll figure: 199 ft. 2,480 + 199 = 2,679 ft [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]].

items.q: Paved runway, 2,400 lb, 2,000 ft, 10 °C: the chart ground roll is 1,035 ft. You have a 4-knot tailwind. The note adds 10% for each 2 knots. What is the ground roll?
Your takeoff distance is 1,100 ft. You add 10% to the gross weight. Using the PHAK rule of thumb, what is the minimum new takeoff distance?
items.why: A 10% weight increase gives at least a 21% longer takeoff: 1,100 x 1.21 = 1,331 ft [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]].

items.q: The PHAK example airplane at VX gains 1,000 ft while covering 3,000 ft over the ground. At that same angle, how much height has it gained after 600 ft of ground distance?

activities.title: Climb away, or settle back?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.
buckets: Can put you back on the ground

items.t: Lowering the nose gently to hold the wheels just clear
Accelerating in ground effect to at least VX
Reducing angle of attack to reach normal airspeed before leaving ground effect
Using the manufacturer's takeoff speed when conditions are marginal
Pulling up out of ground effect below VX
Letting the nose drop too far after lift-off
Forcing it off with too much back pressure before flying speed
A sudden lull in gusty wind at normal takeoff speed

activities.title: Which left-turning effect?
activities.intro: Tap a name, then the clue that matches it.

pairs.r: Loads the left main wheel; depends on the ground surface
Strongest at high propeller speed and low forward speed
A pitch change produces a yaw
Down-moving blade bites harder at high angle of attack
The correction that keeps you straight on the roll

activities.title: Soft-field takeoff in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Correct the performance chart and finish the checklists on firm ground
Roll onto the runway without stopping and line up
Add full power smoothly and check the engine gauges
Hold a nose-high attitude so the wings take the weight
Let the airplane fly itself off at a low airspeed
Lower the nose gently and accelerate in ground effect to VX
Climb at VX until the trees are cleared
Pitch for VY, then retract the flaps

activities.title: Decisions off the grass
activities.intro: You are flying N4128S, a single-engine airplane, on a commercial training flight from a 3,000-foot dry turf strip. Corrected numbers show a 1,524-ft ground roll and 2,679 ft to clear 50 feet. Trees stand at the far end. Flaps are set as the POH recommends.

steps.s: You finished the checklists on the firm run-up pad. You are taxiing toward the runway, where the turf looks soft.
options: Stop on the runway to recheck the checklist
Roll onto the runway without stopping and line up
Hold the brakes at the end and run to full power
Taxi with the nose-wheel pressed down for steering
steps.why: Keep continuous motion with enough power while lining up; stopping on a soft surface can bog the airplane down [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

steps.s: Power is up and the nose-wheel is dragging through the grass. Acceleration feels slow.
options: Push forward to lower drag
Add back-elevator pressure for a nose-high attitude
Tap the brakes to straighten out
Pull the throttle back to reduce P-factor
steps.why: Back pressure sets a positive angle of attack and takes weight off the nose-wheel, so the wings carry the weight and surface drag drops [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

steps.s: The airplane lifts off on its own, well below VX, and keeps rising.
options: Keep climbing to get away from the surface
Retract the flaps to cut drag
Lower the nose gently to stay just above the surface
Reduce power to stop the climb
steps.why: Lower the nose with the wheels just clear and stay in ground effect until at least VX; leaving it early can settle you back even at full power [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

steps.s: You reach VX in ground effect. The trees are ahead.
options: Pitch for VX and hold it within 5 knots until the trees are cleared
Pitch for VY right away
Hold the airplane low until well above VY
Climb at the lift-off speed for the steepest angle
steps.why: Climb at VX until the obstacle is cleared [[24:145|AFH 6-13]], within ±5 knots (ACS CA.IV.C.S10).

steps.s: The trees pass well below you. You are climbing through 250 feet.
options: Raise the flaps all at once, then pitch for VY
Pitch for VY, then retract the flaps in steps
Reduce to climb power before anything else
Stay at VX to pattern altitude
steps.why: After clearing the obstacle, adjust pitch to VY and retract gear and flaps [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]; raising flaps in increments avoids a sudden loss of lift [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

steps.s: At 400 feet the engine loses power. You are still holding right rudder.
options: Turn back to the strip
Hold the climb attitude and try a restart
Lower the nose at once, center the rudder, and land mostly straight ahead
Raise the nose to trade speed for height
steps.why: At climb attitude without power you are near a stall. Lower the nose immediately, coordinate with rudder, and glide to a landing area, preferably straight ahead [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

final_quiz.q: You depart a strip covered in wet slush. Positive rate of climb, VY, no obstacles. What does the AFH say about the landing gear?
options: Retract it at once to cut drag
Leave it down briefly so the slush can air-dry
Retract it only after reaching cruise altitude
Cycle it twice quickly to shake off the slush
final_quiz.why: With wet snow or slush on the surface, do not retract the gear immediately, so the slush can be air-dried [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

final_quiz.q: On a crosswind soft-field takeoff, you hold full aileron into the wind early in the roll. What should you expect from performance?
options: Better acceleration, because the wing is unloaded
No change until lift-off
Less takeoff performance, because the deflected controls add drag
A shorter roll, because the upwind wing lifts first
final_quiz.why: With ailerons and rudder deflected, drag increases, so expect less initial takeoff performance until you are wings-level and coordinated in the climb [[24:138|AFH 6-6]].

final_quiz.q: Winds are 210 at 15 gusting 25 down a grass runway. What does the AFH advise about lift-off speed in strong, gusty wind?
options: Obtain an extra margin of speed before leaving the ground
Lift off even slower than normal to stay in ground effect
Use the normal lift-off speed exactly
Lift off at VX and climb steeply out of the gusts
final_quiz.why: In strong, gusty wind, get an extra margin of speed before leaving the ground; a sudden lull at normal takeoff speed can cost positive control or cause a stall [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

final_quiz.q: Your corrected grass ground roll is 1,524 ft and the POH landing ground roll is 700 ft. About how much runway does the AFH method say you need to accelerate and stop?
options: About 1,524 ft
About 2,224 ft
About 2,679 ft
About 3,048 ft
final_quiz.why: Add the takeoff and landing ground rolls: 1,524 + 700 = 2,224 ft [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

final_quiz.q: Sample chart, 2,400 lb, 5,000 ft, 30 °C: ground roll 1,620 ft, total over 50 ft 3,160 ft. The strip is 3,200 ft of dry grass with zero wind. Is it enough to clear 50 ft?
options: Yes, 3,160 ft is under 3,200 ft
Yes, grass shortens the roll by adding friction
No, you need about 3,634 ft
No, you need about 3,403 ft
final_quiz.why: 15% of 1,620 = 243 ft. 3,160 + 243 = 3,403 ft, more than 3,200 ft [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]]. Adding 15% of the total instead (3,634 ft) is the common slip.

final_quiz.q: Using the sample chart's wind note, how much do you add to the distances for a 6-knot tailwind?
options: 10 percent
21 percent
30 percent
60 percent
final_quiz.why: Add 10% for each 2 knots of tailwind (up to 10 knots): 6 knots = 3 x 10% = 30% [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]].

final_quiz.q: A larger airplane is departing ahead of you on the same grass runway. How do you avoid its wake?
options: Rotate before its rotation point and climb above its climb path
Rotate after its rotation point and stay below its path
Start your roll at once so you follow it closely
Hold low in ground effect the whole way to the end
final_quiz.why: Note its rotation point, rotate before it, and keep climbing above its climb path until you turn clear of its wake [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

final_quiz.q: Which conditions does the PHAK commonly link with low-level windshear?
options: Clear skies, calm wind and a cool morning
Fronts, thunderstorms, temperature inversions and upper winds over 25 knots
Only mountain waves above 10,000 feet
High pressure with light and variable wind
final_quiz.why: Low-level windshear is commonly associated with passing frontal systems, thunderstorms, temperature inversions and strong upper winds over 25 knots [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

final_quiz.q: At 150 feet after a soft-field departure the engine quits. You are nose-high and still holding right rudder. What are your first two actions?
options: Raise the flaps and turn back to the runway
Hold the attitude and try a restart
Add left rudder and climb to gain time
Lower the nose at once and center the rudder for coordinated flight
final_quiz.why: At a climb attitude without power you are at or near a stalling angle of attack. Lower the nose immediately and move the rudder to stay coordinated, then glide to a landing area ahead [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

final_quiz.q: You climb at VX over trees with soft-field flaps set. When and how should the flaps come up?
options: Right after lift-off, all at once
As soon as you reach VX, all at once
After the trees are cleared and you pitch for VY, in steps
Only after landing at the destination
final_quiz.why: Climb at VX until the obstacle is cleared, then pitch for VY and retract gear and flaps [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. Raising flaps in increments avoids a sudden loss of lift and settling [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

final_quiz.q: Your wingspan is 32 feet. The wing is 8 feet above the grass during the level-off. About how much is induced drag reduced?
options: About 1.4 percent
About 23.5 percent
About 47.6 percent
About 75 percent
final_quiz.why: 8 ft is 1/4 of a 32-ft span, which cuts induced drag 23.5 percent [[1:108|PHAK 5-11]]. 1.4 percent is at one full span, 47.6 percent at 1/10 span (3.2 ft).

final_quiz.q: The Chart Supplement shows your turf runway slopes upward in the takeoff direction. What does that do?
options: Slows acceleration and lengthens the ground run
Shortens the ground run because you climb sooner
Has no effect at low speeds
Only matters for landing
final_quiz.why: An upsloping runway impedes acceleration and gives a longer ground run on takeoff [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]].

final_quiz.q: Your POH lists VX at 62 knots. Climbing over obstacles on your commercial checkride, the airspeed drifts to 68 knots. What is the problem?
options: None; anything from 57 to 72 knots meets the standard
It is outside ±5 knots, and the climb gradient may suffer
None; faster than VX always gives a steeper climb
It only matters if the stall horn sounds
final_quiz.why: The commercial standard is ±5 knots (57 to 67 knots) (ACS CA.IV.C.S10). In some airplanes 5 knots off causes a significant loss of climb performance [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].
